title: Increasing the broad-leaved tree fraction in European forests mitigates hot temperature extremes

settings.description: Generalised additive models linking observed land surface temperature to broad-leaved tree fraction across Europe for 2009-2014, controlling for latitude, longitude, elevation and topography.
SEVIRI hourly land surface temperature product, giving 24 values per month.
MODIS land surface temperature product with four acquisitions per day at approximately 01:30, 10:30, 13:30 and 22:30.
The Atlantic biogeographical region, with an oceanic climate and less limiting soil moisture.
The Mediterranean biogeographical region, with high incoming shortwave radiation and dry summers.
The Boreal biogeographical region, with lower incoming shortwave radiation.
The Alpine biogeographical region, which contains the Swiss in-situ comparison sites.
Summer daytime hours, when the cooling signal is largest.
Nighttime hours, when energy-balance differences between forest types are small.
Winter daytime, evaluated separately and giving region-dependent signs.
Observed daily maximum temperatures separated into quantiles from 0.1 to 0.9 within each biogeographical region.
Ten paired forest and open-land in-situ sites in Switzerland measuring 2 m air temperature within the canopy.
The annual mean temperature response, in which seasonal and diurnal cycles largely average out.

claims.from: broad-leaved tree fraction increase from 10 to 90 per cent
claims.statement: An increase in broad-leaved tree fraction induces summer daytime cooling in all five biogeographical regions.

claims.from: broad-leaved tree fraction increase in the Atlantic region
claims.statement: The cooling is largest in the Atlantic region, reaching up to 2 K in August.

claims.from: broad-leaved tree fraction increase in the non-Atlantic regions
claims.statement: In the four other regions the summer cooling lies roughly between 0.5 and 1.5 K.

claims.from: broad-leaved tree fraction increase
claims.statement: At night there is a slight warming effect throughout the year in every region except the Mediterranean.

claims.from: broad-leaved tree fraction increase in winter
claims.statement: In winter, daytime cooling or warming occurs depending on the region.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. A seasonal sign ambiguity, so the extracted claims imply an unconditioned cooling.

claims.from: choice of MODIS or SEVIRI land surface temperature product
claims.statement: The MODIS and SEVIRI signals strongly agree for most regions despite differing resolutions and retrieval methods.

claims.from: choice of land surface temperature product in the Mediterranean
claims.to: magnitude of the summer daytime cooling
claims.statement: In the Mediterranean the summer daytime cooling is much larger for SEVIRI, up to 1.5 K, than for MODIS, up to 0.85 K.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. A measurement-dependent magnitude disagreement.

claims.from: averaging over the seasonal and diurnal cycles
claims.statement: Seasonal and diurnal cycles largely average out, so the annual mean temperature response in several regions is close to zero.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. Without it, the extracted cooling claims read as an annual-mean benefit, which the paper explicitly denies.

claims.from: using the two MODIS Aqua observations per day
claims.to: estimate of the annual mean effect
claims.statement: The two MODIS Aqua observations per day can roughly approximate the annual mean effect of an increasing broad-leaved tree fraction.

claims.from: broad-leaved rather than needle-leaved forest
claims.to: timing of the daily maximum temperature
claims.statement: Daily maximum temperatures occurred earlier over broad-leaved than over needle-leaved forests in most regions.

claims.from: higher daily maximum temperature quantile within a region
claims.statement: Within each biogeographical region the summer cooling effect is larger for higher daily maximum temperature quantiles.

claims.from: background temperature across regions
claims.statement: Cooling potential is related to background temperature within a region but not between regions: the Mediterranean is hottest yet cools less than the Atlantic and similarly to the Continental region at high quantiles.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. This blocks the naive transfer rule that hotter places gain more.

claims.from: temperature quantiles between 0.6 and 0.9 in the Mediterranean
claims.to: summertime cooling from increased broad-leaved fraction
claims.statement: In the Mediterranean the summertime cooling hardly increases between the 0.6 and 0.9 quantiles, plausibly because soil moisture limitation attenuates the evapotranspiration difference.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. A saturation threshold that matters for dry-region transfer.

claims.from: 80 per cent increase in broad-leaved tree fraction
claims.to: daily maximum temperature during the hottest days
claims.statement: The reduction of daily maximum temperatures during the hottest days reaches up to 1.8 K in the Atlantic region and up to 1.5 K in the Continental and Mediterranean regions.
claims.match_note: Not extracted; the headline magnitudes for hot extremes are absent even though the generic quantile relation was captured.

claims.from: magnitude of the broad-leaved tree fraction increase
claims.statement: Land surface temperature decreases approximately linearly with the increase in broad-leaved tree fraction, so a moderate increase still has substantial impact.
claims.match_note: Not extracted, so no partial-adoption scenario can be scaled from the graph.

claims.from: in-situ paired-site observations in Switzerland
claims.to: the remote-sensing diurnal, seasonal and quantile results
claims.statement: In-situ observations corroborate that the cooling potential increases from lower to higher summer daily maximum temperatures and agree with the Alpine diurnal and seasonal cycles.

claims.from: in-situ station analysis versus remote-sensing analysis
claims.to: sign of the nighttime temperature signal
claims.statement: Station data suggest lower nighttime temperature for broad-leaved trees while the remote sensing analysis shows a very weak or slightly positive nighttime signal.

claims.from: broad-leaved tree fraction increase
claims.to: summer daily maximum temperature difference between forest and open land
claims.statement: An increase in broad-leaved tree fraction decreases the summer daily maximum temperature difference between forest and open land.

claims.from: higher albedo and larger latent heat flux of broad-leaved trees
claims.statement: The authors attribute the lower summer temperature over broad-leaved forest to a larger reflected shortwave fraction and a generally larger latent heat flux from higher stomatal conductance.
claims.match_note: Not extracted, so the extracted temperature claims carry no mechanism.

claims.from: lower incoming shortwave radiation in boreal forests
claims.statement: The moderate boreal cooling signal is attributed to lower incoming shortwave radiation reducing the temperature impact of the higher broad-leaved albedo.

claims.from: drought-adapted traits of Mediterranean broad-leaved species
claims.to: evapotranspiration difference between broad- and needle-leaved species
claims.statement: Mediterranean broad-leaved species have evolved smaller leaves and lower evapotranspiration rates, so the evapotranspiration contrast with needle-leaved species is potentially smaller there.

claims.from: less limiting soil moisture in the Atlantic region
claims.statement: Because soil moisture is less limiting in the Atlantic region, physiological differences in evapotranspiration between broad- and needle-leaved species become more prominent there.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. This is the condition that explains why the Atlantic region cools most.

claims.from: earlier stomatal closure in coniferous species
claims.to: afternoon cooling advantage of broad-leaved trees
claims.statement: Conifers close stomata earlier than many deciduous broad-leaved species, giving a stronger latent heat decline over needle-leaved forest and hence greater broad-leaved cooling in the afternoon.
